memory_update.text: AI should be tracked as an infrastructure funnel: demand and inference monetization pull hyperscaler/neocloud capex, which pulls accelerators, HBM, advanced packaging, networking, servers, data-center sites, power, cooling, and construction execution.
Power access, grid interconnection, substations, transformers, and switchgear are the highest-scored AI physical bottleneck in this Layer 2A pass.
HBM and advanced packaging remain high-confidence semiconductor chokepoints because AI accelerator supply depends on memory qualification, stacking yield, packaging capacity, and customer allocation.
AI networking and rack-scale integration are rising chokepoints as next-generation platforms shift from individual accelerators to full AI-factory systems.

Key recurring catalysts to monitor: hyperscaler capex guidance, AI cloud backlog/utilization, HBM4 qualification and allocation, next-generation accelerator platform ramps, data-center power deals, and export-control changes.
Need a focused Layer 2B check on which public companies have verifiable revenue exposure to each bottleneck node versus merely thematic exposure.
Need cross-check of non-official capex estimates against company filings and transcripts before using any aggregate 2026 hyperscaler capex number as a hard fact.

Need project-level evidence for data-center delays, including interconnection queues, transformer lead times, water constraints, and local permitting opposition, before ranking construction and utility beneficiaries.
NVDA is the highest-directness AI infrastructure relationship in this chunk because Vera Rubin spans accelerators, CPU, scale-up networking, DPUs and Ethernet switching.
AVGO is a high-priority non-GPU accelerator and AI networking mapping; next validation should focus on named customer exposure and durability of custom ASIC ramps.
SK hynix/000660.KS is the HBM chokepoint mapping; HBM4 qualification, yield and allocation are the key evidence tracks.
CRWV is a pure-play AI cloud capacity monetization mapping with strong backlog and NVIDIA Rubin validation evidence, but customer concentration and financing risk remain core checks.

MSFT, AMZN, META and ORCL are demand-side capex converters whose AI thesis depends on turning infrastructure spending into cloud, model and enterprise AI revenue without unacceptable margin compression.
DELL is the deployment-layer server/rack integration mapping; AI server backlog and shipments are strong, but margin quality and working-capital intensity require follow-up.
WCC, NVT and MOD represent second-order physical-infrastructure mappings for data-center electrical distribution, liquid cooling and cooling systems.
For WCC, NVT and MOD, Layer 3 should separate AI-specific data-center demand from general data-center, utility, commercial construction and HVAC demand.

For all tickers in this chunk, later layers still need market-pricing checks: valuation, estimate revisions, gross-margin sustainability, capex intensity, balance-sheet risk and customer concentration.
For accelerator and HBM names, next evidence should connect Vera Rubin and custom ASIC ramps to HBM4, advanced packaging, substrates and foundry capacity constraints.

FIX should remain in the AI physical-buildout cluster, but its relationship is an inference until technology/data-center and AI-specific backlog contribution is quantified from filings or investor materials.
DLR has strong direct evidence for AI-oriented hyperscale capacity via Q1 2026 record bookings, backlog and management language about hyperscale AI-oriented U.S. capacity.
CAT has unusually explicit AI infrastructure evidence for an industrial name: Q1 2026 Power Generation growth tied primarily to data-center applications plus a 2 GW hyperscale AI power agreement.
EME maps to mission-critical AI data-center buildout and skilled labor, but exact data-center or AI backlog share must be extracted before upgrading from inference to fact.
EQIX maps to AI through interconnection, xScale and advanced cooling, but its exposure is broader enterprise/cloud digital infrastructure rather than a pure AI data-center capacity play.
TT maps to the AI thermal bottleneck after LiquidStack, with direct-to-chip and immersion cooling complementing Trane's broader data-center thermal portfolio.
CRM has measurable enterprise AI monetization evidence through Agentforce and Data 360 ARR; later layers should isolate organic Agentforce growth from Data 360/Informatica contribution.

NOW has measurable AI adoption evidence through Now Assist customers above $1 million ACV and broader Autonomous Workforce positioning, but product efficacy and implementation friction remain important falsification checks.
For the physical-infrastructure names, next layer should normalize AI exposure by revenue/backlog percentage, lead times, margins and customer concentration rather than relying only on thematic fit.
For CRM and NOW, next layer should test whether AI ARR/ACV is incremental paid monetization or packaging/upsell attached to existing platform renewals.

summary: Split Layer 2 synthesis. Layer 2A initial industry-chain map for the AI theme as of 2026-06-07. The current AI chain is best framed as an infrastructure-and-monetization funnel: enterprise and consumer AI demand pulls hyperscaler/neocloud capex; capex pulls accelerators, custom ASICs, HBM, advanced packaging, networking, servers, optical interconnect, data-center construction, power, cooling, and grid interconnection; software monetization and inference utilization determine whether the buildout remains economically justified. Highest Serenity chokepoint nodes in this pass are power/grid access, HBM/advanced memory, accelerator supply, advanced packaging, AI networking/scale-up interconnect, and data-center construction/cooling execution. This is research mapping only, not a trading recommendation.

supply_chain_map.node: End-user AI demand and enterprise agentic workflows
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Paid enterprise adoption converts model capability into recurring software, cloud, and inference demand. If agentic workflows show measurable productivity or ARR contribution, they support continued infrastructure spending; if not, the capex cycle becomes more fragile.

supply_chain_map.node: Frontier model training and post-training demand
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Large model training, synthetic data generation, reinforcement learning, and post-training workloads create demand for dense GPU/ASIC clusters, high-bandwidth memory, scale-up networking, and large power blocks.

supply_chain_map.node: Inference serving and AI application runtime
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Inference is the recurring usage layer. Token volume, latency requirements, context length, and agentic task complexity determine whether data-center utilization and AI cloud revenue can catch up with capex.

AI demand becomes revenue only after capital budgets are converted into GPUs/ASICs, servers, networking, data-center shells, power, and customer-ready capacity. Delays in any upstream layer push out monetization.

supply_chain_map.node: AI accelerators: GPUs, custom ASICs, and rack-scale compute platforms
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Accelerators remain the central compute input for training and inference. Supply depends on leading-edge wafers, HBM availability, advanced packaging, substrate capacity, networking, and system integration.

HBM is tightly coupled to AI accelerator performance and supply. Qualification cycles, TSV stacking, yield, packaging coordination, and customer allocation make HBM one of the hardest-to-expand AI supply nodes.

supply_chain_map.node: Advanced packaging, CoWoS-like capacity, substrates, and interposers
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: High-end AI accelerators require dense packaging of GPU/ASIC dies, HBM stacks, interposers, substrates, and thermal interfaces. Packaging capacity can constrain accelerator shipments even when wafer supply exists.

supply_chain_map.node: Leading-edge foundry wafers and semiconductor equipment
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: AI accelerator and custom silicon supply depends on advanced-node wafer starts, lithography, etch/deposition/metrology tools, yield learning, and geopolitically concentrated manufacturing footprints.

supply_chain_map.node: AI networking: NVLink-scale-up, InfiniBand, Ethernet, DPUs, switches, SerDes
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Training clusters and AI factories are networked computers. Scale-up and scale-out networking determine cluster efficiency, utilization, and ability to serve large models at low latency.

supply_chain_map.node: Optical interconnect, transceivers, silicon photonics, and CPO pathway
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Bandwidth and power efficiency pressure increases with rack density and cluster size. Optical modules and future co-packaged optics can become bottlenecks if electrical interconnects hit power or distance limits.

supply_chain_map.node: AI servers, rack integration, ODM/OEM assembly, burn-in, and acceptance
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Accelerators must be integrated into reliable rack-scale systems before customers can use them. Rack power, cabling, firmware, liquid-cooling readiness, logistics, and acceptance testing can delay revenue readiness.

supply_chain_map.node: Data-center land, shell capacity, leasing, and colocation
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: AI clusters require large contiguous power blocks, entitled land, shell capacity, network access, and fast commissioning. Scarcity shifts pricing power toward sites with pre-secured power and permits.

supply_chain_map.node: Power generation, grid interconnection, substations, transformers, switchgear
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Power access is increasingly the gating input for AI data-center growth. Long interconnection queues, transformer/switchgear lead times, transmission limits, and ratepayer politics can slow deployments even when chip supply improves.

supply_chain_map.node: Thermal management: liquid cooling, rear-door heat exchangers, CDU, chillers
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Higher rack densities push cooling from traditional air toward liquid and hybrid systems. Cooling readiness can decide whether next-generation racks can be deployed at planned density.

supply_chain_map.node: Construction execution, skilled electrical/mechanical labor, commissioning
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Data-center capex is constrained by real-world project execution: EPC capacity, electricians, mechanical contractors, permitting, safety, component logistics, and commissioning schedules.

supply_chain_map.node: Energy policy, permitting, export controls, and national-security regulation
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Policy can accelerate or restrict the chain through federal land access, power permitting, nuclear/generation support, AI security rules, and export licenses for advanced chips.

supply_chain_map.node: Model platforms, AI cloud marketplaces, and developer distribution
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Cloud platforms and model marketplaces shape where inference demand lands and which infrastructure providers capture utilization. Distribution affects the pass-through from AI adoption to compute revenue.

supply_chain_map.node: Corporate customers, governments, healthcare, financial services, defense
supply_chain_map.why_it_matters: Regulated and large-enterprise customers require security, compliance, data governance, reliability, and ROI proof before broad AI deployment. Their adoption determines the durability of downstream software demand.

ticker_relationships.next_evidence: Validate liquid-cooling revenue scale, backlog by product, hyperscaler customer exposure, CDU/PDU margin, capacity ramp execution and competitive overlap with Vertiv, Schneider, Eaton and private vendors.
ticker_relationships.node: Liquid cooling, enclosures, power distribution and rack infrastructure
ticker_relationships.relationship: nVent maps to high-density AI rack physical infrastructure; disclosures point to data-center momentum, liquid cooling demand, manufacturing expansion, and participation in NVIDIA Vera Rubin reference architectures.

ticker_relationships.next_evidence: Quantify AI-specific data-center revenue, air versus liquid cooling mix, backlog visibility, capacity expansion timing, margin sustainability, customer concentration and competition from Vertiv, Schneider, Johnson Controls and private cooling vendors.
ticker_relationships.node: Data-center cooling and thermal management
ticker_relationships.relationship: Modine maps to the thermal-management bottleneck created by high-density AI data centers; filings cite AI-fueled data-center growth and cooling-solution demand.

ticker_relationships.next_evidence: Pull FIX May 2026 investor presentation and latest 10-Q; extract technology/data-center revenue percentage, modular backlog, customer concentration, margin by segment, and whether management specifically attributes growth to AI data centers rather than broader technology projects.
ticker_relationships.node: Data-center construction execution / mechanical and electrical systems / modular construction
ticker_relationships.relationship: Comfort Systems USA maps to the capex-conversion layer: hyperscaler and AI data-center capex becomes usable compute only after mechanical, electrical, modular, service and commissioning work is completed. Current evidence supports a strong construction/backlog relationship, but exact AI-specific exposure still requires validation.

ticker_relationships.next_evidence: Track megawatts under construction, percentage pre-leased, lease commencement lag, power availability, incremental development capital, hyperscale customer concentration, and renewal pricing.
ticker_relationships.node: Hyperscale AI data-center capacity / colocation / power-land bottleneck
ticker_relationships.relationship: Digital Realty maps directly to the AI physical-capacity layer. Its leasing, backlog, hyperscale AI-oriented capacity and power-constrained campuses determine how quickly AI demand converts into operational data-center capacity.

ticker_relationships.next_evidence: Separate durable AI data-center power demand from cyclical oil/gas and industrial power demand; track Power & Energy orders, backlog, lead times, data-center-specific disclosures, emissions/permitting constraints, and margin impact from manufacturing costs.
ticker_relationships.node: Behind-the-meter power / backup generation / prime power for AI data centers
ticker_relationships.relationship: Caterpillar maps to the time-to-power bottleneck. If grid interconnection delays persist, AI data-center operators may rely more on large reciprocating engines, turbines, generator sets, microgrids and related power services.

ticker_relationships.next_evidence: Use EMCOR Q1 2026 presentation and filings to quantify data-center, network-and-communications, semiconductor and high-tech manufacturing backlog; compare organic growth, margin mix, labor availability and project execution risk.
ticker_relationships.node: Mission-critical electrical/mechanical construction / network and communications / skilled labor bottleneck
ticker_relationships.relationship: EMCOR maps to the buildout labor and execution layer, where mission-critical electrical, mechanical and network infrastructure can gate AI data-center completion. Evidence supports a strong backlog and network/communications relationship, but AI-specific backlog purity is not yet fully proven.

ticker_relationships.next_evidence: Track xScale megawatt deployment, enterprise AI use cases, AI-related bookings, liquid-cooling availability, power density, interconnection growth, and whether AI workloads lift pricing or capex intensity.
ticker_relationships.node: Interconnection-rich colocation / xScale hyperscale capacity / distributed enterprise AI infrastructure
ticker_relationships.relationship: Equinix maps to AI deployment through interconnection, cloud adjacency, xScale hyperscale deployments and data-center capacity for enterprises and service providers. Exposure is strategic but less pure than power-constrained hyperscale shell capacity because EQIX also serves broad digital infrastructure demand.

ticker_relationships.next_evidence: Quantify data-center revenue and orders after LiquidStack and Stellar Energy integration; track direct-to-chip deployments, liquid-cooling attach rates, margins, customer wins and whether AI rack density shifts demand from traditional HVAC to liquid systems.
ticker_relationships.node: Data-center thermal management / liquid cooling / heat rejection / controls
ticker_relationships.relationship: Trane Technologies maps to the AI rack-density and cooling bottleneck. The LiquidStack acquisition gives Trane direct-to-chip and immersion-cooling exposure, complementing chillers, heat rejection, controls and central-plant capabilities needed for high-density AI data centers.

ticker_relationships.next_evidence: Track Agentforce ARR, Data 360 ARR excluding acquired Informatica Cloud ARR, work units, attach rates in large deals, net retention, pricing, customer ROI evidence and risk of AI-native competitors compressing seat-based software economics.
ticker_relationships.node: Enterprise AI monetization / agentic AI applications / CRM data layer
ticker_relationships.relationship: Salesforce maps to the AI demand-validation layer because Agentforce and Data 360 ARR provide measurable enterprise AI monetization evidence beyond product announcements. The thesis depends on paid adoption, retention and expansion rather than infrastructure scarcity.

ticker_relationships.next_evidence: Track Now Assist ACV, customers above $1 million ACV, renewal/expansion impact, autonomous-workflow case studies, implementation success rates, AI billing transparency and whether customers prefer external AI tools integrated into ServiceNow instead of native Now Assist.
ticker_relationships.node: Enterprise workflow automation / AI agents / AI control tower
ticker_relationships.relationship: ServiceNow maps to enterprise agentic workflow adoption, where AI is monetized through Now Assist, autonomous workflow products and platform expansion. Evidence supports strong AI-related customer spend, but product efficacy, governance, pricing clarity and implementation friction remain key falsification areas.
